# XsdToStruct: embed a `XmlStructLoader.load` precompile workload in generated modules

## Context

`XsdToStruct.jl`'s own `@compile_workload` (added earlier, `src/XsdToStruct.jl:150-158`) only warms
`xsd_to_struct_module` itself — the XSD-reading/codegen pipeline. It does nothing for the modules
*generated by* that pipeline. Measured directly (fresh `julia` process per case, `--project`
identical, `basic_types.xsd`/`.xml`):

| step | cold time |
|---|---|
| `include()` the generated struct module alone (no XML involved) | ~0.53s |
| `XmlStructLoader.load(xml, module_path)` against that same fresh module | ~3.7s |

So struct-definition compilation is only ~14% of a generated module's real cold-start cost. The
other ~86% is `XmlStructLoader`'s generic algorithm (`type_in_module`, `get_base_field_type`,
`construct_xml_node_child_objects`, ...) specializing against that schema's brand-new concrete
types — which only happens by actually running a document through `load()`.

**Goal**: every module `xsd_to_struct_module` generates should carry its own
`PrecompileTools.@compile_workload` that exercises `XmlStructLoader.load` against a sample
instance of that specific schema, so the expensive specialization is already compiled by the time
a real caller loads real data. The burden is on `XsdToStruct.jl` — no caller-supplied sample XML,
no opt-in flag.

## Key unlock: `validate=false`

`XmlStructLoader.load(...; validate=false)` skips `AbstractXsdTypes.check_restrictions` entirely
(confirmed: `xsd_module_builder_simple.jl`'s generated inner constructor only calls
`check_restrictions` `if __validated`). This means the synthesized sample instance only needs to
be **type-parseable** (right shape of string per Julia target type) — it does not need to satisfy
min/max, digits, pattern, or enumeration restrictions. This removes the need for any kind of
constraint-solving/regex-instance-generation logic; a single hardcoded dummy literal per built-in
Julia type is sufficient.

The workload calls the `load(io, module_ref::Module)` overload directly (not the
path/module-symbol overload), passing `@__MODULE__` from inside the generated module. This means
the synthesized instance's root tag name is irrelevant — no namespace-prefix or module-symbol
guessing is needed at all.

## What gets synthesized

A new pass walks the same `ComplexTreeNode`/`FieldData` tree the struct-writer already walks (no
parallel tree-walking logic to keep in sync), building an XML string bottom-up from the schema's
root type:

- **Built-in scalar field** → one hardcoded dummy literal per target Julia type (e.g. `"0"` for
  numeric types, `"false"` for `Bool`, `"2000-01-01"` for `Date`, `"x"` for `String`/base64Binary).
- **Nested complex field** (`sub_module` set) → recurse, emit one child element.
- **`is_vector` field** → emit exactly one element (enough to exercise the Vector-append
  construction path; not N — this is a compile-time warm-up, not a load-time perf benchmark).
- **`can_be_missing` (optional) field** → omitted entirely. This exercises the "absent optional
  field" path (the common case in real documents) and sidesteps needing a value for fields with
  no obvious synthesis rule (notably `xs:any`'s `AnyContent` string field, which XmlStructLoader
  treats as an ordinary named field with no special wildcard handling — see
  `xsd_reader_complex_node.jl:89`).
- **`ChoiceFieldData`** → synthesize only `choice_options[1]`; omit the rest.
- **`GroupFieldData`** → resolved the same as a nested complex field (confirm at implementation
  time whether groups are already flattened into ordinary `FieldData` upstream of this pass).
- **Element attributes (`__xml_attributes`)** → explicitly out of scope. `getattributes_dict` is a
  flat, schema-independent operation (same function/dict type for every schema) — it doesn't
  benefit from per-schema warm-up the way the type-dispatching functions above do, so there's no
  reason to synthesize attribute values just to exercise it.

Synthesis itself has no fallible path (every branch has a default) — it always produces *some*
string. Whether that string is actually accepted by `XmlStructLoader.load` for a given schema's
edge cases is handled at the next layer down:

## Failure handling

The emitted `@compile_workload` block wraps its `load()` call in a silent `try/catch`:

```julia
@compile_workload begin
    try
        XmlStructLoader.load(IOBuffer(SAMPLE_XML), @__MODULE__; validate = false)
    catch
    end
end
```

If synthesis produces something `load()` rejects (an unanticipated schema shape — deep recursion,
unusual `xs:any` placement, etc.), the generated module still defines every struct correctly and
still works at runtime; it simply misses the extra precompilation for that one schema. Chosen over
a "detect which schemas are safe to synthesize for, upfront" capability check because it's simpler
and can never regress a schema that used to generate fine — worst case is a silent gap in warm-up
coverage, not a broken module.

## New dependency footprint

Every generated module's top-level file gains, unconditionally:
- `import PrecompileTools` (or `using PrecompileTools: @compile_workload`)
- `import XmlStructLoader` (qualified access only — `XmlStructLoader.load(...)` — not `using`,
  matching this codebase's existing convention of avoiding export-name collisions, e.g.
  `XmlStructLoader.jl`'s own `import XsdToStruct`)

This applies even to callers who never call `load()` themselves on the generated module — accepted
tradeoff, since there's no opt-out flag. The generated docstring's existing "dependencies needed"
list (`xsd_module_builder_top.jl`'s `write_docstring_part`) gets `XmlStructLoader` and
`PrecompileTools` appended alongside the existing `AbstractXsdTypes`/`Reexport` entries.

`XsdToStruct.jl`'s own `Project.toml` is **not** affected — it doesn't itself `using` these
packages, it only emits text that references them. The generated module is what needs them
available in whatever environment it's `include()`d into.

## Where this lives

New file `XsdToStruct.jl/src/xsd_module_builder/xsd_module_builder_precompile.jl`, following the
existing one-file-per-concern convention (`xsd_module_builder_top.jl`, `_struct.jl`, `_simple.jl`,
...). Two responsibilities:
- `synthesize_sample_xml(root_field, xsd_module_builder)::String` — the recursive tree-walk above.
- A `write_precompile_workload_part` function, wired into `write_top_module_to_io`
  (`xsd_module_builder_top.jl`) alongside the existing `write_struct_module_part` /
  `write_meta_module_part` calls, emitting the `import`s, the `const SAMPLE_XML = """..."""`
  literal, and the `@compile_workload` block itself.

## Testing / verification

- **Correctness**: generate a module from an existing fixture (e.g. `basic_types.xsd`) into a
  tempdir, confirm the generated file contains `@compile_workload` and the embedded sample, and
  confirm a subsequent real `load()` call against real fixture XML still returns correct values
  (i.e. running the synthetic workload during precompilation leaves no contaminating state).
- **Performance**: same fresh-process A/B methodology already used to validate
  `XsdToStruct.jl`'s own workload (git-stash before/after, single cold `@elapsed` per process, not
  a warm Chairmarks loop) — measure `XmlStructLoader.load` cold-call time against a freshly
  generated module before and after this change, on at least `basic_types` and one
  larger/nested/choice-bearing fixture (e.g. `documentation_example` or `choice_element`).
- Run the full 5-package test suite as the final gate (per this project's standing convention).
